concept: MongoDB Database Tools: mongodump, mongorestore, mongoimport, mongoexport, mongostat, mongotop, bsondump, mongofiles

claims.text: mongoimport accepts JSON, CSV, and TSV input; JSON is the default. mongoexport exposes JSON and CSV output formats; its documented --type choices do not include TSV. (high confidence)
mongoimport CSV parsing follows RFC-4180: backslashes are not escape characters, and a double quote inside a quoted field must be escaped with another double quote. (low confidence)
The locked percentage is a legacy global write-lock field that appears only against MongoDB versions before 3.0. (low confidence)
If the dump contains no data files matching --nsInclude, mongorestore restores no data for that requested namespace. (high confidence)

For a replica-set backup, mongodump --oplog captures writes during the dump; mongorestore --oplogReplay applies the captured operations after restoring the data. Capture ends when mongodump finishes and does not cover later writes. A directory dump stores the captured operations in oplog.bson. (high confidence)

For a restore without oplog replay, --nsInclude selects matching namespaces and --nsExclude removes matching namespaces. Both accept asterisk patterns. Exclusion takes precedence when both match. The documented command selects transactions.* while excluding transactions.*_dev. (high confidence)

The --oplogLimit timestamp is an exclusive upper bound: mongorestore omits entries with timestamps greater than or equal to it. It requires --oplogReplay, and MongoDB warns that manually selecting oplog entries can cause corruption or inconsistencies. (low confidence)

Treat higher concurrency as a workload-dependent tuning option. The reference says insertion workers may improve speed, while MongoDB support guidance recommends changing concurrency when resources are not already maxed out and notes that restore must recreate data files and indexes. (medium confidence)

Compression trades CPU work for less output I/O: MongoDB support guidance says --gzip can reduce disk-write I/O when CPU is available, while the historical TOOLS-997 reporter says gzip CPU usage made backups take longer. Neither establishes a universal restore-speed gain from gzip. (medium confidence)

In the MongoDB community performance discussion, Stennie says --gzip can reduce dump-write I/O when CPU is available, while restore must recreate data files and rebuild indexes. The advice is to adjust restore concurrency when resources are not already maxed out; these are conditional tuning choices. (low confidence)

mongoexport defaults to Relaxed Extended JSON v2. Use --jsonFormat=canonical when BSON type fidelity matters; mongoimport recognizes Canonical input without a corresponding import-mode flag. (high confidence)

TideWave says Canonical JSON round-trips every type exactly. The Extended JSON specification explicitly limits arbitrary BSON round trips because of ordering and dollar-prefixed wrapper ambiguity; interpret the blog claim as guidance about explicit type representation, not a universal round-trip guarantee. (medium confidence)

Plain JSON directly represents only a subset of BSON types. Canonical Extended JSON emphasizes type preservation; Relaxed mode emphasizes readability and interoperability and can lose type information when converted to BSON. (low confidence)

mongostat normalizes operation statistics to average operations per second even when the polling interval exceeds one second. Read operation rates separately from connection counts and memory snapshots. (low confidence)
mongostat set gives the replica-set name when applicable; repl gives member state: PRI primary, SEC secondary, REC recovering, UNK unknown, RTR mongos router, and ARB arbiter. (low confidence)

mongostat --discover can return statistics for all members when connected to a sharded cluster through mongos; the examples also combine --discover with --interactive for a non-scrolling view. (low confidence)
CloudThinker uses mongotop as a per-collection, per-interval workload view and separates queued readers/writers from active readers/writers when reading mongostat. (low confidence)
mongostat vsize reports process virtual memory and res reports process resident memory, documented in megabytes at the last call. conn reports the total number of open connections. (low confidence)

Use mongodump --version in the operating-system terminal to inspect the installed Tools version. MongoDB recommends the latest release and provides the Tools through its Download Center. (high confidence)

Use the MongoDB Download Center and select the platform and architecture before selecting the package. The installation guide provides Linux deb, rpm and tgz paths, macOS Homebrew and zip paths, and Windows MSI and zip paths. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Use --nsFrom and --nsTo together to rename matching namespaces during restore. Each option requires its matching counterpart. (low confidence)

To restore a sharded-cluster dump, the documented procedure stops balancing, creates and pre-shards destination collections with the source shard keys, restores through mongos while excluding config.*, and restarts balancing. Using --drop after pre-sharding removes the sharding configuration. (low confidence)

Use --nsFrom with --nsTo to rename namespaces during restore. Asterisk replacements correspond linearly between the two patterns; dollar-delimited wildcard variables support nonlinear replacements. These options perform namespace renaming. (high confidence)

GridFS splits files into chunks, using a default chunk size of 255 KiB, with a final chunk only as large as necessary. It uses separate collections for file chunks and metadata and can store files larger than the 16 MiB BSON document limit. (low confidence)
`get_regex` downloads files matching a regular expression and cannot use `--local`; a multi-filename `get` also cannot use `--local`. (low confidence)

The current overview documents Database Tools 100.20.1 as supporting MongoDB Server 9.0, 8.3, 8.2, 8.1, 8.0, 7.0, 6.0, 5.0, 4.4 and 4.2. It explicitly says connections to servers earlier than 4.2 fail. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

In DDEV issue 35 on February 11, 2026, a maintainer reported that the Debian Bookworm MongoDB 8.2 ARM64 repository lacked mongodb-database-tools while Ubuntu Noble had it. The reported build error was "E: Unable to locate package mongodb-database-tools". This is a dated repository-availability report, not a claim that all ARM64 platforms are unsupported. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-11)

For the documented Database Tools 100.20.1 release, MongoDB explicitly excludes Server versions earlier than 4.2 and says connection attempts to earlier versions fail. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
mongodump --archive=<file> writes a single binary archive; --archive without a filename writes to stdout. It cannot be combined with --out. (medium confidence)
mongodump --archive cannot be combined with --out. (low confidence)

mongoexport normally writes one JSON document per MongoDB document; --jsonArray writes one enclosing array. The mongoimport --jsonArray option accepts that form and its reference documents an import limit of 16 MB or smaller. (high confidence)

DRIVERS-3456 demonstrates a dollar-date field collision: an embedded document containing a date-looking string becomes a BSON Date after an Extended JSON round trip. This is an attributed encoding limitation, not evidence that every dollar-prefixed key corrupts data. (medium confidence)
For CSV or TSV input, --headerline uses the first row as field names; otherwise mongoimport imports that row as a document. --headerline produces an error for JSON input. (low confidence)

Extended JSON v2 cannot distinguish type-wrapper keys from user fields with the same names; DBRef is an exception to the documented warning about dollar-prefixed keys. In CSV, periods denote hierarchy, so a literal period in a field name can be misread as nesting. (low confidence)
`bsondump` is a system-command-line tool for viewing and debugging BSON files as human-readable JSON. MongoDB describes it as a diagnostic tool rather than a data ingestion tool. (high confidence)
`--local` selects a local filename for upload or download when it differs from the GridFS name; multi-file get cannot use this option. (high confidence)

Without `--replace`, `mongofiles put` adds another GridFS object with the same name instead of overwriting an existing one. `--replace` changes this behavior; the Kali-distributed help describes removing other same-name files after put. (high confidence)

Starting with MongoDB 4.4, Database Tools have a release cycle separate from MongoDB Server and use their own versioning, initially 100.0.0. Match a Tools release to its compatibility guidance rather than matching its version number to the server. (high confidence)

The MongoDB overview documents Database Tools 100.20.1 and lists support for Server 9.0, 8.3, 8.2, 8.1, 8.0, 7.0, 6.0, 5.0, 4.4 and 4.2. This is a version-specific support list, rather than a requirement to install a Server-matching Tools version. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The mongodump archive format interleaves collection data, allowing concurrent collection backup and restore through a single file or stream; it is a special-purpose format rather than a tar archive. (medium confidence)

For a single-collection restore, mongorestore -j maps to --numInsertionWorkersPerCollection rather than --numParallelCollections. Explicit long flags make the intended concurrency control clear. (low confidence)

mongoexport CSV requires --fields or --fieldFile to select columns. It writes field names as a header by default; --noHeaderLine suppresses that header. Use mongoimport --headerline to consume a CSV or TSV header as names rather than data. (high confidence)

Canonical Extended JSON is not an unconditional guarantee of arbitrary BSON document round trips: reserved dollar-prefixed field names can collide with type wrappers, and the specification also notes JSON object ordering differs from BSON ordering. CSV dots denote nesting and therefore can misinterpret literal dots in field names. (high confidence)
For WiredTiger, flushes counts checkpoints triggered between polling intervals. This field is an interval count rather than a checkpoint-duration measurement. (low confidence)

vsize reports process virtual memory, whereas res reports process resident memory. The reference describes these as memory amounts at the last mongostat call, rather than operation rates. (medium confidence)
`bsondump` formats output as Extended JSON v2.0 in Canonical mode. (low confidence)
For a local BSON file, `bsondump --outFile=collection.json collection.bson` writes readable JSON to collection.json. (high confidence)
`bsondump` reads standard input and writes standard output by default; `--bsonFile` and `--outFile` select explicit input and output paths. (high confidence)
mongofiles provides command-line operations between local files and GridFS, including upload, download, listing, searching, and deletion. (high confidence)
GridFS divides files into chunks and metadata collections; its default bucket uses `fs.chunks` and `fs.files`, with default chunks of 255 KiB. (low confidence)
`mongofiles -d=records put 32-corinth.lp` uploads the local file, while `mongofiles -d=records get 32-corinth.lp` downloads it. (low confidence)
`list` accepts an optional filename prefix; `search` finds filenames matching a pattern within the name. (high confidence)

GridFS does not support multi-document transactions or atomic updates of an entire file. MongoDB recommends uploading a new version, atomically switching a metadata field that marks the latest version, then removing old versions as needed. (low confidence)

`mongofiles` moves files between the local filesystem and GridFS from the system command line. Its syntax is `mongofiles <options> <connection-string> <command> <filename or _id>`. (medium confidence)

`mongofiles -d=records list` lists files in the records database. `list` optionally filters by filename prefix; `search` finds matching filenames, with the Kali-distributed help identifying its argument as a regex. (medium confidence)

`mongofiles -d=records put 32-corinth.lp` uploads a local file; `mongofiles -d=records get 32-corinth.lp` downloads the named GridFS file. `--local` supplies a different local filename for put or get. (medium confidence)
For authorized access, MongoDB documents the `read` role for `list`, `search`, and `get`, and `readWrite` for `put` and `delete` on the accessed database. (low confidence)

The 100.20.0 changelog, released October 26, 2026, states that support for pre-4.2 servers and dump files was removed; both the target server and dump files must be from 4.2 or later. (low confidence)

Separate releases do not require a separate installation in every environment: installing MongoDB Server through Homebrew also installs the Database Tools. The standalone Homebrew package is mongodb-database-tools. (high confidence)

For a standalone macOS Homebrew installation, add the official tap with brew tap mongodb/brew and install with brew install mongodb-database-tools; the installation guide also instructs users to trust the tap with brew trust mongodb/brew. (high confidence)

On Linux, select the distribution and architecture in the Download Center. The installation guide offers a local .deb package installed with apt, an .rpm package installed with yum, or a .tgz archive. (low confidence)

On Windows, install the separate Database Tools MSI or extract the Zip archive and copy the binaries from its bin directory. Add the directory containing the Tools to PATH to invoke them by name. (low confidence)
Database Tools commands run in the operating-system command line. They are not commands to enter inside the MongoDB shell. (high confidence)

The third-party Setup MongoDB Database Tools GitHub action documents an exact-version input, published SHA-256 verification, and a check that mongodump reports the requested version before caching the installation. These are the action author's documented behaviors. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

On macOS, the official Homebrew tap supports installing Database Tools alone: run brew tap mongodb/brew, then brew install mongodb-database-tools. The official repository describes this as a separate installation from Server and shell. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Separate Tools releases do not imply a separate manual install is always needed. The installation guide says a Server install through a system package manager may already include Tools; the official Homebrew repository explicitly says mongodb-community includes them. (medium confidence)

For Windows MSI and zip installations, the guide instructs users to add the installation or copied-binary directory to PATH so the tools can run by name. A successful installation alone does not establish that a command prompt can resolve the executable. (low confidence)

The official Homebrew repository states that uninstalling mongodb-community does not uninstall the bundled Database Tools; removing Tools requires a separate brew uninstall mongodb-database-tools command. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

mongorestore --oplogReplay requires a full member dump created with mongodump --oplog. Do not combine it with --db, --collection, --nsInclude, --nsExclude, --nsFrom, or --nsTo. The implementation explicitly rejects includes, excludes, and namespace renames. The community thread also corrects a suggestion to use nsInclude with replay. (high confidence)

Sharded clusters do not support mongorestore --oplogReplay. mongodump --oplog is not a supported way to capture a sharded-cluster backup through mongos; the mongodump reference says it has no effect there and directs users to the dedicated sharded procedure. (high confidence)

The documented sharded-cluster dump procedure requires stopping the balancer, writes, and schema transformations. It stops balancing, locks the cluster via mongos, takes the dump through mongos, then unlocks and restarts balancing; its consistency condition requires following the steps exactly with no operations in progress at the start. (low confidence)

In its July 25, 2016 explanation, Percona identifies different shard backup completion times as a consistency problem: capturing each shard oplog only until its own dump finishes does not cover a common completion point. The article describes coordinating oplog recording until the last shard finishes; this historical explanation does not establish current support for replaying directly to a sharded cluster. (low confidence)
Without --oplog, a mongodump taken while writes continue does not represent a single moment in time. (low confidence)

mongodump --excludeCollection and --excludeCollectionsWithPrefix require a database specified through --db or the URI; repeat either option to exclude multiple collection names or prefixes. (low confidence)

mongodump --oplog fails if collection renames, aggregation with $out, mapReduce, user/role/privilege changes, or cluster-wide setting changes such as setDefaultRWConcern occur during the dump. (low confidence)
The documented sharded-cluster dump procedure needs MongoDB support for fsync locking through mongos: MongoDB 7.1, or the backported releases 7.0.2, 6.0.11, and 5.0.22. (low confidence)

mongodump --gzip compresses individual files in directory mode and compresses the archive or stream in archive mode. Directory output uses .gz suffixes; --archive and --gzip can be combined. (medium confidence)

Restore a gzip-compressed directory with mongorestore --gzip; restore a gzip-compressed archive with both --gzip and --archive=<file>. The tools do not require a separate manual decompression step for these inputs. (medium confidence)
mongodump --numParallelCollections (short option -j) controls the number of collections dumped concurrently and defaults to 4; it is collection-level parallelism. (medium confidence)

mongorestore --numParallelCollections (short option -j) defaults to 4 concurrent collections; --numInsertionWorkersPerCollection defaults to 1 concurrent insertion worker per collection. Increasing insertion workers may improve large restore workloads. (medium confidence)
mongorestore --maintainInsertionOrder also enables --stopOnError and forces the insertion worker count per collection to 1, limiting insertion concurrency. (medium confidence)

mongodump --archive=<file> writes a single binary archive; bare --archive writes stdout. mongorestore --archive=<file> reads an archive, and bare --archive reads stdin. A mongodump --archive | mongorestore --archive pipeline can stream the data. (medium confidence)

mongodump --gzip compresses directory-mode files individually; --gzip with --archive compresses archive output. Restore a compressed directory with mongorestore --gzip, and a compressed archive with mongorestore --gzip --archive=<file>. (medium confidence)

Canonical Extended JSON preserves explicit numeric type information, whereas Relaxed Extended JSON uses ordinary JSON numbers for integers and finite doubles and can lose numeric type distinctions. (high confidence)
Extended JSON uses a $oid wrapper for ObjectId and a $numberDecimal wrapper for Decimal128 in both Canonical and Relaxed modes. Relaxed mode does not remove every BSON type wrapper. (low confidence)

mongoimport expects Extended JSON v2 Canonical or Relaxed input by default; use --legacy for Extended JSON v1 input. Legacy regular-expression representations can otherwise be interpreted as ordinary embedded documents. (high confidence)

CSV and TSV do not carry BSON type metadata. Use --columnsHaveTypes with typed fields from --fields, --fieldFile or --headerline; declarations can select string(), int32(), int64(), double(), decimal(), boolean() and date formats. The option does not apply to JSON input. (high confidence)

For typed CSV dates, date(<arg>) aliases date_go(<arg>) and uses a Go reference-time layout. An ISO-looking cell alone is insufficient: a reported import with an empty date() argument failed type coercion, and the answer supplied a layout template. (medium confidence)
mongoimport only supports UTF-8 input files; other encodings produce errors. (low confidence)

The tool reference and the TideWave guide disagree about the default --parseGrace setting: the reference says stop, while TideWave labels autoCast as the default. Treat the reference as authoritative; explicitly choose a policy for typed CSV/TSV coercion failures. (medium confidence)
mongoexport defaults to Extended JSON v2 Relaxed mode. Set --jsonFormat=canonical to produce Canonical mode. (high confidence)

For rich BSON type preservation in JSON interchange, use Canonical Extended JSON. mongoimport recognizes the format in the input file, including Canonical output from mongoexport. This recommendation remains subject to field-name and Extended JSON representation restrictions. (high confidence)

Canonical Extended JSON represents BSON integer types with $numberInt and $numberLong string-valued wrappers. Relaxed mode represents them as JSON integer values, so the representation does not retain that integer-width distinction. (low confidence)

CSV export requires an explicit field list through --fields or --fieldFile. mongoexport includes a CSV header by default; --noHeaderLine suppresses it and is valid only for CSV output. (low confidence)

CSV and TSV can carry explicit import types: combine --columnsHaveTypes with --fields, --fieldFile, or --headerline and specify each field as <colName>.<type>(<arg>). --columnsHaveTypes is invalid for JSON input. (high confidence)

For typed CSV imports, date() uses the Go time.Parse layout. The official example specifies birthdate.date(2006-01-02), alongside string(), boolean(), int32(), and binary(base64) fields. (high confidence)

For CSV or TSV type-coercion failures with --columnsHaveTypes, --parseGrace defaults to stop. Alternatives are autoCast, skipField, and skipRow; autoCast can change the resulting field type. --parseGrace has no effect for JSON input. (low confidence)

mongostat gives an instance-level status overview; mongotop locates read and write activity at the collection level. Use the two views together to relate node pressure to busy collections. (medium confidence)
The operation columns report inserts, query operations, updates, deletes, cursor-batch getmore operations, and commands per second. (medium confidence)
An asterisk on the insert value denotes a replicated operation. On a secondary, command values separated by a pipe represent local|replicated commands. (low confidence)

For WiredTiger, dirty is tracked dirty bytes divided by maximum configured cache bytes; used is current cache bytes divided by maximum configured cache bytes. Both are cache percentages, so interpret them against the configured WiredTiger cache. (low confidence)

mongostat qr and qw are queue lengths for clients waiting to read and write; ar and aw count active clients performing reads and writes. The paired output headings qrw and arw distinguish queued from active readers and writers. (high confidence)
netIn and netOut measure incoming and outgoing network traffic in bytes, including traffic generated by mongostat itself; conn is the total number of open connections. (low confidence)

mongotop time values are milliseconds. ns combines database and collection names; total is time spent operating on the namespace, while read and write report time spent performing the respective operations. The timestamp dates the returned data. (medium confidence)
mongotop reports active namespaces or databases. If a collection or database is absent, the documentation says it has received no recent activity. (low confidence)
mongotop --json adds operation counts for the polling interval to the timing data. (low confidence)

mongotop --locks is historical: it reports per-database locks only for MongoDB 2.6 or older and errors on 3.0 or newer instances that do not expose that data. In this mode db replaces ns, and database name . denotes the global lock. (low confidence)
mongostat -o selects the output columns; -O adds serverStatus fields after the defaults. The options are mutually exclusive. (medium confidence)

For custom numerical serverStatus columns, .rate() reports the per-second change and .diff() reports change since the previous sample. The official examples demonstrate both in the -o field expression. (medium confidence)

The historical Stack Overflow discussion cautions that operation-rate interpretation depends on the server configuration and cluster architecture; its example throughput numbers are not universal capacity limits. (low confidence)

The mongostat inserts field counts inserted objects per second; query, update and delete count operations per second. getmore counts cursor-batch operations per second. An asterisk after an insert value denotes a replicated operation; secondary command values use local|replicated. (low confidence)
mongostat netIn and netOut describe received and sent network traffic in bytes, including traffic generated by mongostat itself. (low confidence)

mongotop reports read and write activity per collection and accepts a reporting interval in seconds; its default reporting interval is one second. Use its per-collection view to locate where read and write time is concentrated. (high confidence)

Historical lock fields need server-version context: mongostat locked appears only for pre-3.0 servers. mongotop --locks needs MongoDB 2.6 or older and errors on MongoDB 3.0 or newer servers that do not report per-database lock usage. (high confidence)
